commit.message:
Use thin LTO for PGO training (#29271)

## Summary

Use thin LTO for the instrumented release executable in the PGO build,
while keeping fat LTO for the final executable. Pass the override
through `cargo rustc` so dependency compilation and the workspace's
release profile are unchanged. Debug builds are unchanged.

This reduces the estimated PGO pipeline time by 54% in a Linux x86-64
comparison, with essentially unchanged final binary size and no
consistent runtime regression across the holdout projects used for the
original PGO work in #27570.

## Build results

| Measurement | Fat training | Thin training |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Instrumented build | 487.86 s | 85.50 s |
| Final fat-LTO build, median | 247.75 s | 250.43 s |
| Estimated complete PGO pipeline | 738.02 s | 338.26 s |
| Final stripped executable, median | 22.719 MiB | 22.724 MiB |

Instrumented builds were measured once per mode. Final build times and
sizes are medians of three independently collected profiles per mode.
Pipeline estimates add the instrumented build, median training and
profile merge, and median final build; corpus downloads are excluded.
These are clean local build measurements, not CI timing predictions.

## Runtime results

We trained on the canonical 618-file corpus and evaluated linting and
formatting on Django, pandas, scikit-learn, SciPy, and SymPy, whose
repositories are disjoint from the training corpus. The holdout pins
come from the contemporaneous Windows follow-up in #27573, since the
initial Linux PR did not record exact holdout revisions.

Each case used three independent profile pairs and 12 interleaved
fat/thin timing pairs per profile, for 720 timed runs in total. Runs
used eight pinned CPUs and eight threads, with balanced execution order
and warm caches. Diagnostics and formatting diffs were checked
separately from the quiet timed commands and matched across all six
final binaries.

Positive changes below mean thin training was slower. Intervals are
per-workload hierarchical bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, resampling
profile pairs and then paired timing observations; they are not adjusted
for multiple comparisons.

| Holdout | CPU change (95% CI) | Wall change (95% CI) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Django lint | -0.21% [-0.77%, +0.49%] | +0.10% [-1.41%, +1.29%] |
| Django format | -0.10% [-1.18%, +0.72%] | -0.27% [-1.37%, +1.45%] |
| pandas lint | -0.01% [-0.45%, +0.39%] | -0.67% [-2.49%, +1.26%] |
| pandas format | -0.26% [-1.10%, +0.67%] | -0.84% [-2.81%, +2.12%] |
| scikit-learn lint | +0.02% [-0.62%, +1.12%] | -0.02% [-1.11%, +1.86%]
|
| scikit-learn format | -0.52% [-2.14%, +0.62%] | -0.79% [-2.08%,
+1.03%] |
| SciPy lint | -0.21% [-0.70%, +0.43%] | -0.64% [-4.59%, +1.52%] |
| SciPy format | -0.52% [-1.03%, +0.13%] | -2.47% [-6.20%, +1.61%] |
| SymPy lint | +0.01% [-0.30%, +0.27%] | -0.77% [-3.23%, +0.88%] |
| SymPy format | -0.18% [-1.89%, +1.84%] | -0.58% [-3.58%, +3.30%] |

A longer SymPy formatting repeat with the same three profile pairs and
48 timing pairs per profile measured -0.18% CPU [-1.96%, +1.66%] and
-0.28% wall time [-2.19%, +1.58%]. Individual profiles varied in both
directions, so the near-flat average should not be interpreted as
identical performance for every trained binary. The pandas formatting
wall-time interval remains inconclusive at a 2% slowdown threshold.

All six profiles had matching function/CFG identities and counter
layouts, with no missing-profile or profile-mismatch compiler
diagnostics. Their counter values and `.profdata` bytes were not
identical.

Measurements used the Rust/Cargo source at
`7c6f8fc8fc5655dfa47e125b05453007b9e7a6c7`, the standard release
codegen-unit settings, and Ohm Rust 1.99.0-dev (`08bbd755a`, LLVM
23.1.1) with experimental defaults disabled. The benchmark was not rerun
on this PR's newer base revision. This is an exploratory Linux x86-64
study with three profiles per mode, not a guarantee of zero runtime cost
or equivalent results on macOS, Windows, or ARM.
